- How to challenge your negative self-talk | Josh Green | TEDxSurrey: Kind: captions Language: en Transcriber: Andrew Farrell Reviewer: Raúl Higareda Hello, everyone. (Cheers) This probably just looks like regular old juggling to you, and that’s because it is. (Laughter) But it’s in dropping the ball that I made such a profound discovery, during what I thought was one of the worst and most embarrassing moments of my life. You see, when I was little, I wanted nothing more than to be an actor when I grew up, because the weight of the world hadn't yet crushed my spirit. I hadn’t heard “no” enough. Hadn’t heard that I was too small, too short, too fat, too stupid. Hadn’t heard that I was not smart enough, or not fast enough, or simply not good enough. And because I hadn’t heard some of this until much later in my life, I started the journey of getting myself an agent. It was through that process that I started to hear some of those more negative comments. “You’re not ready.” “You’re not the right look.” “You’re just not good enough.” And I started to internalize this, unfortunately. So I had to start in the safest place. I got myself a background agent, which required nothing more of me than to stand still in the background. Kind of like the child that plays the tree in the school play, but just happy to be on the team. One day, though, my agent did call me with my very first audition. No more tree for me. She calls me and she says, “Hey, you can juggle, right?” To which I respond, “Yes, of course.” “Great. Your audition is tomorrow, 9 a.m. sharp. Toodles.” My agent loved to say “toodles.” Now, I’d like to make something abundantly clear. At that point in my life, I didn’t know how to juggle. Like, at all. So I did what anyone would do in a situation like that. I called my friend Adam, who does. I show up at his house at 5:00 p.m. and he starts me off with scarves, slow-moving juggling scarves so my body has time to figure out what it’s doing. Then he upgrades me to my first ball. Then two. And finally three. And by the end of the night, I’m able to juggle for about five seconds. It doesn’t look pretty, and I make a lot of strange focused faces as I’m doing it. But you can technically call it juggling. The next day I show up at the audition on time and it is packed with professional jugglers, clowns, and magicians, all of whom are nonchalantly carrying on full conversations while juggling six balls at the same time. They’re bouncing them off the walls, they’re so good, and I’m just in awe, staring at my borrowed juggling balls. And in come these voices. “You are not good enough.” “You don’t belong here.” All I want to do in this moment is disappear and make sure I don’t embarrass myself or my agent so badly that I’m never able to work in this town again. But I take a deep breath, remember that I have a whole five seconds of juggling under my belt, and I sit down. And then I hear it, “Josh, Josh Green, you’re up.” (Shouts) On the inside. Such grace and confidence on the outside, even though clearly sweating through my shirt. I walk into the audition room, introduce myself to the casting directors, and wait for them to call action. I start juggling. I’ve got my struggle face on, I’m biting my tongue in fierce concentration, and I’m moving all over the place. I’m about to reach my five-second juggling limit, and they haven’t stopped me yet. Why haven’t they stopped me? Then it happens, I drop the ball. At this point, my face couldn’t look sillier. I’m staring at them, they’re staring at me. I don’t know what to do, so I just pick the ball up and continue juggling as if nothing ever happened, trying to smile through my struggle face. They stop me immediately. “Thank you, that’s enough. Next.” And in come those voices again. “I told you you weren’t good enough, you blew it.” The next day, my agent calls me, asking me how I thought it went. I tell her that I gave it my best shot, and we’ll get them next time. I thought she’d give me a little bit of feedback, but instead she says, “You nailed it, you got the part.” Wait, what? So she emails me the script with the name of my character at the top of the page, and in bold letters it says, “Stupid Jester.” (Cheers and applause) In sharing this story with you, you got a really good look of what was going on for me externally, but I’d love to dig into the discoveries I made internally to help me navigate some of those really negative voices. The first one: those voices, they’re not your voices. No child is born thinking they're not enough. The voices we hang on to tend to come from a select few people in our lives, a teacher, a parent, a bully, a partner. They start on the outside and they slowly move inside, but they’re not our voices. They’re somebody else’s and we don’t have to listen to them. And guess what? The casting directors have those voices too. They were given so much information from so many people just saying they needed somebody who could juggle. They also have superiors, so they wonder, “Am I doing a good job? Am I getting the right person?” The person interviewing you probably feels this way. Your date might feel that way as well. No one really knows exactly what they're looking for, which is why Steve Jobs so famously said, “Nobody knows what they want until you give it to them.” Which is why, after a long day of amazing jugglers, all pretty much doing the exact same thing, being amazing, I walked in, looked like an idiot, to which they responded, “Oh my gosh, this guy’s perfect.” Another discovery I made was practice. I did not just show up to my first audition, overcome my negative thoughts and I lived happily ever after. No, no, no. I practiced, I started safe and small. I started as a background performer. All I had to do was walk around in the background and make it look so uninteresting that it didn’t draw anyone’s attention. What's the safest place that you could start? What’s your version of background performer? Because once you start, it builds momentum that can’t be stopped. But you do have to start. You also have to show up. I had so many chances to turn down my juggling opportunity. I could have told my agent that I didn't know how. I could have just not gone to the audition. And I could have just left when I saw all the amazingly talented jugglers that were there. But I stayed in spite of the voices that said I wasn’t good enough, and I showed up because I could have been exactly what they were looking for, and I was. Had I not gone, though, the show would have gone on without me. They would have cast another juggler in the role, and it would have been fine. But that means somebody else would be living my life right now. Ask yourselves, how many people are living your best life because you turned down an opportunity? So say yes to opportunities. Show up. You probably also noticed that I didn’t do this by myself. Though I didn’t know how to juggle, I did know someone who did. Surrounding myself with extremely talented people who know more than me and think highly of me has always been so helpful at helping me expand my horizons, or in this particular instance, growing me out of a pinch. Think of all the people in your life and what they could show you if you called them and said, “Can you teach me how to play guitar, or how to swim, or whatever a project manager does.” One of the most painful discoveries I made during all this was that it’s not all rainbows and sunshine. There is a harsh truth that I had to get through. Books and movies tend to skip over these parts, but the truth is, as a background performer for over two years before I got my first audition, the voices were very loud back then, extremely cemented and internalized. After that, I only landed one in every 30 auditions, one in every 50 jokes got a laugh while I was on stage, and I failed more businesses than I care to remember. This is why it’s so important to start safe, keep practicing, continue to show up, and have the support of others, because all of these proactive actions over time help to silence those negative voices. It pushes them further away, and it all leads to a much more fulfilling life. Saying yes to acting led to a wonderful and fulfilling acting career. Saying yes also led to a comedy career that allows me to travel the country. It allowed me to be on the bottom of the ocean on just one breath for over two minutes. It allowed me to save a human life, that was pretty cool, and to doing my very first TEDx. (Applause) All of this because I embraced the moments when those voices arise. So look, I know that the unseen life is a scary life, so we tend to stick to what’s safe because it keeps those voices quiet. When I took on five hours of juggling to do my first audition, I kept hearing, “No way you’re going to be good enough.” But I embraced the part of me that felt like I couldn’t do it and said, “Why wouldn’t I be good enough?” I practiced, I showed up, and I took my place, and I encourage you to do the same. Because when you hear that voice that says you’re not good enough, that just means you’re doing something right. It means you're embracing the human experience and pushing yourself just beyond your edge. So let’s be honest, dropping the ball does not sound like a good idea, but it’s one of the best things that ever happened to me. So the next time opportunity comes your way, and you hear a voice saying, “You’re not good enough, don’t drop the ball,” I encourage you to do the exact opposite. Thank you.

- Analytics in YouTube Studio: Kind: captions Language: en YouTube Studio provides at-a-glance and in-depth analytics to help you analyze your videos and your channel. From the dashboard, you can see the performance of your latest video compared to your typical video performance. You'll see how it ranks against your last 10 videos along with its views, average view duration and watch time. The channel dashboard also provides a quick glance at your overall channel analytics. Here, you'll see your current subscribers a summary of your views and watch time in the last 28 days and your top videos from the last 48 hours. Let's look at the Analytics page, where you can deep-dive into all your data. You can do so for your channel as a whole for a video group or for a specific video by clicking into a video or searching for it. From an individual video, click the back arrow to head back to your overall channel analytics. Note that anywhere in Analytics, you can change the date range you want to look at. Consider ranges of 90 or more days in order to get a sense of long-term performance trends. You can also hover over any metric in Analytics get to more info about it. Or, you can click the See More button on any card to review additional data or to compare different metrics time periods videos or groups. Click the X in the top-right corner to go back. The Overview tab is your starting point for any channel performance reviews. It provides personalized insights about your channel's performance and gives a high-level look at key performance stats like views, watch time, subscribers and, if you're in the YouTube Partner Program estimated revenue. You'll see insights on how each metric is doing compared to your typical past performance and you can click on any of these to update the graph below. This graph charts day-by-day performance changes for the selected metric. The play button icons below the graph indicate any videos published so you can also compare these metrics against your most-recent uploads for the selected date range. The Overview tab also shows the real-time activity for your videos from the last 48 hours and your top videos for your selected time period. You can also see a snapshot of the performance for your last 10 videos similar to what you see in your channel dashboard. If you're looking at a specific video, the Overview tab will show your video's views, watch time, and subscribers gained or added. You'll also see the audience retention likes versus dislikes, and the real-time activity for that video. Aside from the Overview tab, you'll see the Reach, Engagement and Audience tabs. And, if you're in the YouTube Partner Program you'll see a Revenue tab listed in Analytics. The Reach tab is your central source for data on how many viewers you're reaching and how you're reaching them. This includes impressions, click-through rate, and unique viewers. Impressions are counted every time a viewer comes across one of your video thumbnails on YouTube. Click-through rate shows you how often viewers clicked into a video after seeing an impression, which results in a view. And unique viewers shows the estimated number of different people who come to watch your videos over a set time period. The Reach tab also shows various information about your videos' traffic sources and the surfaces driving viewers to your content. Finally, there's the viewership funnel which provides insight into the viewership process starting with serving an impression all the way to how those clicks and views led to watch time. You can increase the chance of YouTube suggesting your content by increasing your click-through rate and video watch time. The Engagement tab provides data on viewer retention, including watch time average view duration, and end screens. Average view duration will give you the estimated average minutes watched per view on a piece of content. This tells you how long viewers are watching a video before moving on to another piece of content. The end screen data here provides information on what end screen elements are best resonating with your audience. At the video level, this is also where you'll find information on audience retention, likes versus dislikes and, if you've added them, the end screen element click rate. You can use the Audience tab of Analytics to learn about who was watching your videos. This tab will show unique viewers, average views per viewer, and subscribers. These metrics combined give you an idea of the size of your audience as well as their level of engagement. You can also see watch time from subscribers. At the channel level, you'll also see the bell notifications card. This informs you about the portion of your subscribed audience who have enabled all notifications for your channel and also those who have enabled notifications for their account and device. This tab also informs you about the viewers watching your channel like their gender, age group, and where they're located. Finally, if you're a member of the YouTube Partner Program Here, you'll be able to review revenue data such as estimated revenue, monetized playbacks, and playback-based CPM. You'll also see your monthly estimated revenue your top-earning videos and a breakdown of your revenue sources and top ad types. This was just an overview of the main tabs in Analytics. So YouTube is trying to keep viewers satisfied, and keep them on their platform by showing them the right content at the right time that they're most likely to engage with and enjoy. Because of that, it's important to make sure that when you are looking at your click-through rate, you're not just looking at the click-through rate number itself, but you're also looking at the watch time that's being generated from your video. So when you are looking at the effectiveness of your thumbnail, what you actually wanna look at is, of course, you wanna look at the number for the click-through rate compared to the impressions that it's getting, because the impressions part is really important, but you also wanna look to see how those impressions led to watch time.   14. @CyclopsDragon: Regarding the question of your chance of getting the optimal run of Carl Goes to Loss Vegas, Norvada: Based on my rudimentary understanding of statistics, the ideal run would be done in four lives, with each one looping through the hubs twice, being broken down as follows:

RNG entrance (FIRST LIFE ONLY): 1/2 chance to enter
First room: <Number of rooms with a coin left>/7 chance to get a room with an available coin
First coin saving hub: The random chance here is irrelevant, because you're going through again on this life, so you don't need to save your coins here
Second room: Free choice, no RNG
Second coin saving hub: 1/2 chance to get sent down the correct path

The trick is that because there's a section you need to go through twice, you want to do it as early as possible, because that means you have more rooms available on future lives. So you do it on your first free choice if you don't happen to get it on your first random chance, resulting in the following random chances in a row:

1/2 to enter
<Three steps with no relevant RNG, gaining two coins>
1/2 chance to save your coins before death 1
6/7 chance to get a room with an available coin
<Two steps with no relevant RNG, gaining two coins>
1/2 chance to save your coins before death 2
4/7 chance to get a room with an available coin
<Two steps with no relevant RNG, gaining two coins>
1/2 chance to save your coins before death 3
2/7 chance to get a room with an available coin
<Two steps with no relevant RNG, gaining two coins>
1/2 chance to get sent to the key door
1/2 chance to dodge the swings (optional)

Putting all these together results in a roughly 0.218% chance for an optimal run, or a roughly 0.437% chance for an optimal run without caring about dodging the swings.

For example, if you're filming a short, funny Instagram reel to post immediately, 1080p is probably more than ideal. But if you're filming a 20-minute travel YouTube video, then 4K would be a better pick and a better picture. Better pick and a better pick. Up next is frame rate. Frame rate refers to the number of shots your camera takes per second when you're filming a video. And like resolution, the best frame rate to choose depends on what your goal of the video is. The higher the frame rate, the smoother and more realistic your video will look. 30 frames per second is generally the standard frame rate for most social media videos, but you might want to consider using 60 frames per second for smoother motion if you're shooting a video with a lot of action. Once you feel comfortable with the resolution and frame rate you've chosen, the next settings to pick are focus and exposure. You can use the auto settings on your phone, but make sure to tap on the main subject in the frame to lock the focus and optimize the exposure. This will help ensure that the subject stays sharp and well lit. Okay, now that you've got most of the camera settings dialed in, the last two that you need to choose are white balance and color accuracy. You can easily calibrate these two things for your shooting conditions by using a white piece of paper and a color checker. Once you understand all of these settings, you can easily fix lowquality footage in less than a minute. And all you need to do is open your camera setting and switch to 4K or 1080p. Select a frame rate based on the type of video that you're making. Tap and hold the subject to lock focus and exposure and then manually adjust the white balance and color setting to match your lighting conditions. If you stick to this process every single time you film a video, you'll be amazed at how much of a difference it actually makes. But it does take practice. So after you watch this video, try filming just a 5-second clip with default settings. Then film another video using all of these tips. Which one looks better? You tell us. I mean, it's so obvious. It's obviously the second one. But we can make it look even more professional with the next step. One of the most important things to remember when learning to film high-quality content is that every video is only as good as its lighting. It doesn't matter how valuable the content of your video is. If the lighting is too poor for viewers to see it, it's not going to make a difference. You also need to pay attention to how you frame your video, which means how you position yourself and your camera in relation to whatever it is that you're filming. The fact of the matter is lighting and framing go hand in hand. And even the most expensive camera in the world will still produce bad videos if these two components of filming aren't done well. So, here's what you need to know about lighting. First, natural versus artificial light. Natural light is all you need if you're filming outside during the day. An especially good time to use natural light is during what's known as the golden hour, which is actually 2 hours of each day. The hour just after the sun rises and the one just before it sets. If you film during this time, your videos will have a nice warm glow. However, if you want soft shadows with even lighting, it's better to film when it's overcast. If you're filming inside, you can use natural light that comes from the windows, but you may need to supplement it with artificial light, which you can introduce with soft boxes, ring lights, or any other light that you use for a controlled indoor setup. The way you position your lighting is also very important. Your most powerful light, also known as your key light, should be placed at a 45° angle from your face. An easy way to think of that is to put it right in front of you and then move it slightly to the left or right. Doing this creates depth from the soft shadows, giving your face a more professional look. You can then use other lights in addition to your key light to fill in shadows or create special effects. But avoid placing a light directly behind you because that'll cause a silhouette or a halo. There are a few cases in which this setup can be useful or expressive, but they are few and far between. Once you have your lighting figured out, it's time to figure out framing and composition. So, how do you position yourself in front of the camera to make the most professionallook video possible? Well, there are a few ways. And again, it totally depends on the goal of your video. When it comes to framing and shot composition, the main thing that you need to know is the rule of thirds. If you're shooting horizontally, the frame can be divided into nine equal sections that are separated by imaginary lines. If you place all of the important parts of the shot along those lines, your video will start looking way more professional. If you want to see these lines on your phone while you're shooting, you actually need to activate it on your phone by going to the camera settings and turning on grid. For the best results, when filming yourself talking to the camera, keep your ey line placement near the top third of the frame. When filming other subjects, whether it's a person or an object, you can always use the rule of thirds as a general guide for creating pleasing compositions. Now, at this point, you may be wondering, should you use a tripod or hold the camera as you film? Tripods obviously give you the most stable footage possible, which is great for tutorials, interviews, podcasts, and reviews. Handheld footage, however, is more dynamic and it works better for vlogs, behind the scenes content, and even action shots. We can take positioning a step further here because the way you position your camera can actually add a lot to the storytelling aspect of your video. Wide shots that capture the entire scene are great for establishing locations and situations as well as creating breathing room in the edit. If you're teaching someone how to do something, an over-the-shoulder angle can be very powerful because the viewer can observe exactly what it is that you're trying to do. Using low angles can be a good way to make subjects look powerful, and using close-ups are a great way to show emotion and detail. They're particularly useful when you want to focus attention on the people or characters in your video. Those are just a few options of framing to go along with your lighting. hesitations in the sequence disrupt the flow of the overall video and it really doesn't take much sometimes I find only leaving a frame or two either before or after the action window can throw off the entire flow of a sequence I like to think of it like I'm driving on a highway and if you're stuck in bumper to bumper traffic and you're stopping and starting and stopping and starting this is Now, most modern road bikes have the gear shifters integrated into the brakes, so brake on the left hand side, well this actually shifts the front mech, changing the big ring down into the small ring. And on the right hand side, the brake, here, that actually shifts the rear mech, so changing from the big cog to the small cog and vice versa. Now, the bigger the cog at the back, the easier the gear, but the reverse can be said for the front. So, the bigger the chain ring on the front, the harder it is to pedal. As clear as mud? We know. When you swing both of the levers inward, so the right and the left, firstly on the right, the lever being swung inwards changes you to a bigger cog at the back, which actually makes it easier. Now on here, I've got electric gears, so I'm just using the paddles. Now, on the left hand side, when you swing the mechanical lever inwards or tap the electric paddle, it makes it or turns onto a bigger cog at the front or chain ring, which is actually harder, and then, when you've tapped the paddles or the button on the mechanical system, the opposite happens. (techno music) - So now you know what lever does what. When should you be using them? Well, for the vast majority of the time, you will be using your right hand to change gears at the back. The reason being that the actual differences between the gears are much smaller back here, so that when you do change gears, actually the rate at which you pedal, or your cadence, changes only slightly. Now, it's only when you get to the extreme ends of those sprockets at the back, so those really big ones or the really small ones, that you then think about using your left hand to change into a different chain ring, and therefore make a bigger jump. The only thing you need to bear in mind with your gears is they are there to help you. They're there to help you pedal at the right cadence. Now, what that might be does very much depend on you, but we'd say generally we want to be looking at about 80 revolutions per minute. - How Do Bike Gears Work? | Bicycle Gears Explained: Kind: captions Language: en - Bicycles have gears to help you ride more efficiently when going uphill, downhill, and on the flat across all varied terrain. Without easy gears, you'd grind to a halt when trying to go up steep hills and without bigger gears, well you wouldn't be able to pedal fast enough when going downhill. But how do gears actually work? Well in this video, we're going to show you. But before we do, if you haven't already, then please subscribe to GCN and also click the bell icon as this'll help you get notifications. We regularly upload content with helpful tips and advice and it helps support the channel. (intense tones) Before we explain how bicycle gears work, we first need to explain the different parts, beginning with the shifters. (upbeat music) These are located on the handlebars and are used to change gear. On older bikes, these used to be located on the downtube here, but on modern bikes, they're on the bars. They can be like this or like this. Next, we have the cassette. This is the collection of different sized cogs or sprockets on the rear wheel. These are the chainrings and they're turned by the pedals. Bikes typically have one, two, or three chainrings. The chain connects the chainrings with the cassette. We then have the derailleurs, one at the back, and if you have more than one chainring, you'll have one at the front too. The derailleurs are called derailleurs because they literally derail the chain, guiding it from one sprocket to the next as they move from side to side. Most derailleurs move from side to side thanks to a cable that is connected to the gear shifter. When you click the shifter, it pulls the cable tighter, which in turn, pulls the derailleur a measured amount up the cassette. This also compresses a spring. To shift down, clicking the shifter releases the tension in the cable and allows the compressed spring to now extend a measured amount to guide the chain into the next gear. The most high tech components don't have cables, but are now self-contained electronic systems. Instead of the cables actuating the gear change, the derailleurs move using little electronic motors called servos. The rear derailleur contains springs and this cage with little pulley wheels in, which help guide the chain and, crucially, keep it under tension. This is important because without it, changing the size of the gear could make the chain slack and then, it would slip. To help with the changing of gears and make it smoother, the teeth on the cassette and chainrings are specially shaped with little ramps to help guide the chain. Bikes have gears to help you with changes in gradient and if desired, to increase speed on the flat. The smallest chainring at the front, paired with the biggest cog at the back, is the easiest gear, ideal for steep climbs or setting off from a standstill. If your chainring has 34 teeth and your biggest cog at the back also has 34 teeth, that is a one to one gear ratio, a relatively easy gear to turn. The rear wheel will turn once for every pedal stroke. At the opposite end, if you shift into your fastest and hardest gear, the ratio is much bigger. For example, if your biggest chainring is 50 and your smallest cog at the back is 11, that results in a ratio of 4.55, meaning the rear wheel will spin 4.55 times for every one rotation of the pedals. This is a harder gear to get going, but is useful once you're traveling at speed or going downhill. I hope you found this video useful and informative and that you now know how bicycle gears work. If you do, then please give it a thumbs up and share it with your mates and if you have any suggestions of things you'd like us to explain in future videos, then let us know in the comment section down below.

- 10 Editing Tips Every Beginner Must Know!: Kind: captions Language: en Most beginner editors are making small mistakes that are costing them views, watch time, and subscriber growth. So, let's dive into these 10 editing tips every beginner must know. You got to just press record. So, our first tip of the day is that your first frame of video really does matter, and you want to be intentional about what you're showing in your first frame of video. And this is typically because YouTube is now actually autoplaying video silently. As somebody hovers over your video, whether on the computer or even on a cell phone, it starts to play that first frame of video instantly. A couple things to avoid here is first and foremost, don't fade in from black or leave a bunch of empty space at the beginning of your video. Those first couple seconds are super valuable. So, just dive right into the content with the first frame. Additionally, there's a lot of data out there to suggest that starting off with stock footage can create sort of a disconnect between you and your viewer. So, ideally, try not to start off with stock footage or any video clip that feels sort of like it's stocky or not inherent to the content of the video. Try to avoid that. Okay, moving right along into our second tip is to add movement to your A-roll. So, the goal here is to just keep up the visual energy throughout your video, especially if you're just talking. If you're just delivering talking head content, if you can add some movement to those A-roll clips to make them feel more interesting, this is going to help drive retention. And this doesn't have to be every section of the script. It can just be maybe every third section. But what you're doing here is just allowing the viewer to have a moment to reset their attention. Take a little breath. Wonder what's coming next instead of trying to have this retention focused editing that's so fast-paced and removes every single silence and every single mistake. it can get a little exhausting for your viewer when you do that kind of editing. And then in your actual editing timeline, you can add a little bit of space between those key sections to add some breath. Our fourth tip is to spend the most amount of time editing your hook. So, this actually starts with pre-production in scripting out your entire hook. So, even if we have a video that's going to be a little bit more off the cuff and we go more unscripted, we will still script at least the first sentence or the first few sentences of our video to make sure that the hook is dialed in. A couple mistakes you want to avoid when editing your hooks would be first and foremost, don't let your hooks be too long. Now, let me explain what those L and J cuts even mean. They actually correspond to the way that a cut visually looks inside of your editing software. An L cut looks like the shape of an L and a J cut looks like a J. So an L cut is when the audio from the previous clip keeps playing just a little bit longer while the video cuts to the next scene. So that audio is going to overlap just a little bit. And then J cut is the exact opposite of that. So that's when the audio from the next video is going to play a little bit before the visuals of that video play. So that creates sort of a J looking cut. Using these L&J cuts to sort of help your audio and your video feel like it's a little bit more smooth and cohesive versus just a standard hard cut where you're just like making a line and you drag the video over and everything's just like a hard cut all throughout your video and nothing's overlapping. That can feel a little bit jumpy at times. So these LJ cuts can help smooth those transitions, especially from one key section to another in your video. So you just kind of got to find the balance of where you want to EQ. Things that keep people watching because they want to... and because they lean into your story. These are simple but powerful secrets. So now I start my edits with only audio before I touch a single clip. Yeah, you really heard that well. But believe me, it will really change your edits. So here's how I do it: for YouTube... I record my hook and my intro voiceover before I even start shooting. then I find music that matches the energy that I have in my head, and I will even add a few sound effects And right away I see where my voice over is too long, where things don't work, or where I should work on the pacing. and even better... And another great thing about this is that once you've shot everything, the edit is already halfway done because the pacing is there, the voiceover is there, and the music is there. So the only thing you basically have left to do is add the shots in. So ,the next video you're working on, lock in your audio first, because you will spot some time issues instantly. And the more you do this, you know, the more your brain will practice creating a story in your head before even filming. And that actually is one of the most useful skills you can build as a filmmaker. If there's one thing that makes or breaks your video, it's pacing. Your edit’s speed is your storytelling pulse. And I think it’s one of the biggest mistakes that I see even from experience editors. It's that they're staying in the same pace for too long. So here are three things that I think really shape pacing. The first one is shot length because short and snappy cuts make things fast or increase the tension, and longer shots are more for emotion or producing calmness. Then the second one is shot motion. You have chaotic handheld movements that can really add energy, or smooth and stable frames that really calm things down. And I think mixing those in the right way can be really strong. And then there's a third, which is music and sound, because your soundtrack really sets the heartbeat as well you know... A driving beat really pushes the story forward and softer music is really what can let it breathe as well. And of course, sometimes... a silence can be really strong as well. Anyway, if you keep the pace high the entire time, people will get overwhelmed. And if it stays slow, they will get bored. So yeah, it's really good to time that change and energy. Because that really snaps the attention back... or it really puts people in the right emotion when you want to. For example, listen to the first 30 seconds of this video. We start with no music. tension rising with a sound effect, then pause for a second, then full energy, quick shots, fast music, then a short break, a longer shot. Tension is building again. Then energy back up with fast cuts. Then we release into slower shots and no music. Finally we settle into a neutral pacing. And that variation is really what keeps a hook like that really alive. So the next time you edit, just spend a little more time on pacing. Just mark your big moments and your quiet moments, and then let your cuts, your movements, and your music flow between them. Your audience... They will stick with you much longer. I'm sure. you know, one of the hardest things, but also one of the most important things about editing is finding music that actually fits the mood of your story. It's all about getting a rough shape down first and then start refining. So if you've already created the hook and the intro of your video with an audio blueprint... then you can use the assembly edit to shape the rest of your story fast. So here's how I do it. First, I spot the footage that tells the story. So spotting just means cut out the junk and keep the clips you will actually use. Then I drag some of them into the timeline in the rough story order, with a beginning, a middle, and an end. And I'm not polishing anything yet. If I already recorded my voiceover, I will drop that in too. And then I spent time finding music that matches the pace. You know, sometimes it’s temporary music, but sometimes I can already find the real track. Then I just play everything back from the beginning to the end, and I can really watch the rough story unfold. And I just really pay attention and immediately I will see where the gaps are, the pacing feels off, or what kind of shots I'm still missing, or sometimes what I can really get rid of. So before you dive into polishing, build your assembly edit. Drag your key clips into a story order and then refine after that. It will save you hours of frustration and I'm sure it will give you way more clarity on where your edit is heading. And where your story is heading. So with my first edits... I loved picking a song and just cutting on the beat. We've all probably done those edits and they feel nice, but it gets repetitive pretty fast. And I think real flow goes way deeper. So here are just a few ways to create flow. The first one cut intentionally. Don't just throw clips together. Just think about where the eyes of your audience are on the screen and how the movements of the eyes flow from one shot to the next, or how one shot flows to the next. Then the second one is beat accents, because instead of cutting on the beat, you can land an action with the beat like when you're dropping something, or when you're stepping in a frame, or even raising an eyebrow... I will show you an example in a bit. , Then the third audio transitions. Because a sound effects across two shots can really glue them together. And sometimes a sound effect does that even much better than the shots themselves. And a combination is even better. So, for example, in the intro of this video, I cut the movement going out of the shot from the right to the left. Then coming in from the right to the left. So it feels fast but smooth. Then I hit beat accents. Me coming on to the desk or raising my eyebrows right on the beat. So instead of cutting on the beat, the action itself matches the beat. So next time you edit... don't just think about speed, think about movements. Where are the eyes going? Where's the rhythm pulling? Just try one intentional cut, maybe one beat accent and one audio transition. And I'm sure your edit will feel much... smoother instantly. if your edit feels predictable, people tune out. And that's why I like to break my own rhythm with a quick sudden cut... or a change of scene, or just something completely unexpected. So that contrast, that's really what can bring people back into your story, even a small surprise creates a little spike of focus. And those tiny spikes are really what keep people watching. As long as it's not too forced and it's part of your story You can use contrast... This can be anything, loud versus quiet or fast versus slow or bright versus dark Or, I add suprise. Just something playful or something abrupt that no one saw coming. 1. Ночь, когда тишина стала невыносимой

3. Отказ от Страха
«Я — не та тишина, которой я стала, я — не тот страх, который произносил мое имя» [05:24, 11:49].

Это ключевой момент дезактивации «пидарасов» внутри неё. Она больше не « shadow of the light» (тень света) [03:00, 09:25], она сама становится этим Светом. «Я была тихой, я была маленькой — теперь я стою во весь рост» [06:40, 13:13].
